post.description:
Exchange credentials for OAuth token
     *
     **Curl Example:**
     * ```bash
     * curl -X POST 'https://pm-api.test.primemover.example/api/v1/auth/token' \
     * -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     * -H 'Accept: application/json' \
     * -d '{
     * "grant_type": "client_credentials",
     * "client_id": "your_client_id",
     * "client_secret": "your_client_secret"
     * }'
     * ```
     *
     **R Example:**
     * ```r
     * library(httr)
     * library(jsonlite)
     *
     * response <- POST(
     * url = "https://pm-api.test.primemover.example/api/v1/auth/token",
     * add_headers(
     * "Content-Type" = "application/json",
     * "Accept" = "application/json"
     * ),
     * body = toJSON(list(
     * grant_type = "client_credentials",
     * client_id = "your_client_id",
     * client_secret = "your_client_secret"
     * ), auto_unbox = TRUE)
     * )
     *
     * token_data <- content(response, "parsed")
     * print(token_data)
     * ```

parameters.name: filter[status_code]
parameters.description: Which bots need attention: a comma-separated status list matched against the crawler's LATEST RUN -- the run with the greatest started_at, ties broken by id, runs that never started excluded so a session composed for tomorrow cannot mask last night's failure. Values are expanded through the alias table, so failure also matches the runs spelled 'failed'. A bot that has never run matches no status. An unrecognised value returns an empty page; an unknown filter KEY is still HTTP 400.

parameters.name: filter[bad]
parameters.description: Shorthand for filter[status_code]=failure,warning -- the contract's is_bad predicate over the crawler's LATEST RUN, expanded through the alias table server-side so no client has to carry it. 1/true/yes/on ask for the bad ones; 0 is 'show me everything' and never 'only the good ones', because that would classify every unknown status as good.

parameters.name: hours
parameters.description: Rolling window, in hours, behind every latest_queues_* count. Clamped to 1..720 rather than rejected; anything non-numeric (or absent) means the 24-hour default.

latest_queues_count.description: Runs this bot started inside the window, whatever their outcome.

latest_queues_succeeded.description: Runs in the window whose own status_code is success (or a legacy synonym).

latest_queues_failed.description: Runs in the window whose own status_code is failure (or the legacy 'failed'). The run produced nothing usable.

latest_queues_warning.description: Runs in the window whose own status_code is warning (or the legacy 'warn'): the run completed but lost jobs along the way. Not a success -- 'needs attention' is failure OR warning.

latest_queues_degraded.description: Runs in the window holding at least one job with status_code warning: job data was not written, or the decision function could not apply a filter the experiment requested. Derived from the JOBS, so a run whose own status is success can be degraded. Overlaps latest_queues_warning without containing it or being contained by it -- never add the two together.

latest_queues_treatment_lost.description: Runs in the window holding at least one job whose decision_treatment_lost is true: the bot was configured to be treated and produced control-arm data anyway, so that session is scientifically void. Such a run is routinely 'success' with every job 'success' -- nothing FAILED. Counted off a three-state column, so 0 means 'no run here is KNOWN to have lost its treatment': every job predating the runner deploy has a NULL verdict.

get.description:
Every video id this crawler's decisions have selected, across all of
     *     its runs and experiments, most recently chosen first. This is the input to the
     *     decision function's already_watched filter: the runner reads it and puts it in the
     *     lambda payload.
     *
     *     Answers 409, NOT an empty list, when jobs.decision_selected_id does not exist. An
     *     empty list is the positive claim 'this bot has watched nothing', and a caller would
     *     then filter nothing while believing it had filtered correctly.

get.summary: Health of one experiment over a rolling window
get.description:
Triage above the bot. An experiment carries no status of its own -- no column, no aggregate -- so answering 'which of my studies needs attention?' used to mean paging through every crawler (15 per page) and summing the rollups client-side. This is that answer in one request and a constant number of grouped queries.
     *
     * Three things worth knowing before reading the numbers:
     *
     * - **Every bucket is alias-aware.** status_code is not a normalised column and the API deliberately never coerces on write, so the same outcome is spelled several ways in one table: 277 queue rows and 256 job rows say failed where the runner now says failure, and skpped is a runner typo that persists. Rows are grouped by the raw value and folded through the alias table, so failure counts all four spellings.
     * - **unknown is a reported bucket, never folded into success.** A NULL status_code, an empty one, and a spelling nobody has an alias for all land there. The six buckets always sum to total.
     * - **bad_runs / bad_jobs are failure OR warning** (docs/integration-contract.md 3.4), never failure alone. warning means the run or job finished having lost something the experiment cares about -- the state nobody would otherwise look at, and the reason the 2026-08 overhaul exists.
     *
     * treatment_lost_jobs and degraded_jobs count VERDICTS off three-state columns (true / false / NULL = unknown). Only true is counted, so 0 means 'nothing here is KNOWN to have lost its treatment' -- a study whose jobs all predate the runner deploy reports 0 while knowing nothing. See docs/integration-contract.md 7.3.

parameters.name: hours
parameters.description: Size of the rolling window, counted back from now over the runs' started_at. Clamped to 1..720 rather than rejected -- this answers a dashboard, and a 400 because someone typed hours=0 would be worse than the one-hour window they nearly asked for. Anything non-numeric (or absent) means 24. The window actually used comes back as window_hours.

200.description: Health of the experiment over the window

window_hours.description: The window actually used, after clamping.

bots.description: Crawlers configured on this experiment. Deliberately NOT window-scoped: it is the denominator that makes the run counts readable.

runs.description: Runs that STARTED inside the window, bucketed by status_code. started_at rather than created_at, because runs are composed ahead of time -- a queue exists, with a future start_at and no status_code, long before it runs.

total.description: The sum of the six buckets below, never counted separately.

warning.description: Completed, but lost work along the way.

unknown.description: Anything that normalises to none of the five: NULL, empty, or an unrecognised spelling. Reported, never counted as success.

jobs.description: Jobs belonging to those runs, bucketed the same way. Scoped through the run's start, not the job's own, so runs and jobs describe the same body of work.

treatment_lost_jobs.description: Jobs whose decision_treatment_lost is true: the bot was configured to be treated and produced control-arm data, so that session is scientifically void. The alarm. Such a job is routinely status_code success -- nothing about it failed.

degraded_jobs.description: Jobs whose decision_degraded is true: a filter the crawler REQUESTED did not apply. 'A human should look at this decision.'

last_finished_at.description: When this study last finished a run, ACROSS ALL TIME -- the one field here that is deliberately not window-scoped, because it is what makes an empty window readable: 'last finished 5 days ago' and 'never ran' are different situations. null means no run has ever finished.

parameters.name: filter[status_code]
parameters.description: Comma-separated list of statuses, each expanded through the alias table: failure also returns the 256 rows this database spells 'failed' (plus 'error' and 'fatal'), skipped also returns the runner's 'skpped' typo. An unrecognised value matches nothing and returns an empty page; an empty value is no filter at all. An unknown filter KEY is still HTTP 400.

parameters.name: filter[bad]
parameters.description: 1 = only the jobs a human should look at, exactly equivalent to filter[status_code]=failure,warning. The contract's is_bad predicate (docs/integration-contract.md 3.4), computed server-side so no client has to carry the alias table -- and so nobody writes it as failure alone, which is how degraded jobs stayed invisible. 0 is a no-op, not an inversion.

parameters.name: sortBy
parameters.description: 'severity' or '-severity': order by what the status_code MEANS -- success 0, skipped 1, running 2, unknown 3, warning 4, failure 5 -- so the four spellings of failure land together and a NULL or unrecognised code ranks above running rather than beside success. Replaces the default -id ordering.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Spatie sort list; accepts the same 'severity' / '-severity' as sortBy, and composes (sort=severity,-id).

status_code.description: Legacy rows also hold 'failed' and 'skpped'; an unrecognised value is unknown and must never be read as success.

decision_degraded.description: The decision function's verdict: a filter this crawler REQUESTED did not apply. NULL MEANS UNKNOWN -- never clean and never false. A job that predates the migration, a job that never called the decision function (most jobs), and a job run by a runner that has not been redeployed are all NULL. Render 'no verdict', not a green tick.

decision_treatment_lost.description: The bot was configured to be treated and produced control-arm data. The alarm: this session's data is scientifically void. Always false for a control crawler; NULL means unknown.

decision_selection_mode.description: 'llm' or 'random'. A NEUTRAL DESCRIPTION of how the video was picked -- 'random' is the correct answer for a control crawler and 82% of measured payloads. NEVER branch on it alone.

decision_report.description: {filters, llm, warnings, applied, requested}. filters[x] == 'skipped' means NOT REQUESTED and is never a failure. GET /jobs/{id}/decision serves the full stored payload, including for jobs that predate these columns.

get.description: Serves the parsed lambda-jobdata payload recorded for this job, straight from the runner's object store. This is what makes the HISTORICAL verdicts readable: the four decision_* columns on the job row only describe jobs run after the runner deploy, while the ~54000 stored objects go back to the start.

200.description: The decision function's response, with the verdict already read off it

data.description: The decision function's own response: xpath, present, selected, procedure, timestamps, warnings and, when the function was new enough to emit them, degraded / treatment_lost / selection_mode / filters / llm.

invocation.description: The runner's envelope: statusCode/success/functionError. These describe the CALL, which is 200 even when every requested filter failed. Never a verdict.

verdict.description: The contract's rules applied once, here, so no client has to reimplement them. reported=false means the payload predates the degradation report and the answer is UNKNOWN, not clean.

404.description: No decision payload was ever recorded for this job

502.description: A payload was recorded and the object store would not give it up. Missing evidence about the job, never evidence that the job was fine.

put.description: Update job status, progress, and results from automation runner

status_code.description: Current job status. 'warning' is terminal: the job ran to completion but something the experiment cares about degraded -- job data was not written, or the decision function could not apply a filter the crawler had requested. A decision answering selection_mode 'random' is NOT on its own a warning: for a control crawler that requested no filter it is the correct answer. Not validated against this list -- an unknown code is stored as sent, so a new runner state can never leave a job stuck at 'running'.

decision_degraded.description: The decision function's 'degraded': a filter the crawler REQUESTED failed to apply, or nothing could be selected. Omit it (NULL) when there is no verdict -- NULL means unknown, never clean and never false.

decision_treatment_lost.description: The decision function's 'treatment_lost': degraded AND nothing requested applied, so a bot configured to be treated produced control-arm data. The alarm. Always false for a control crawler.

decision_selection_mode.description: 'llm' or 'random'. A NEUTRAL DESCRIPTION of how the video was chosen; 'random' is the correct answer for a control crawler and is not an error. Never branch on it alone. Not validated against a list -- an unknown mode is stored as sent.

decision_report.description: {filters, llm, warnings, applied, requested}. filters[x] == 'skipped' means NOT REQUESTED and is never a failure. Shrunk member by member rather than rejected if it exceeds 60000 bytes encoded, and marked _truncated when that happens.

parameters.name: filter[status_code]
parameters.description: Comma-separated list of statuses. Every value is expanded through the alias table, so failure also returns the rows this database spells 'failed', 'error' and 'fatal', and skipped also returns the runner's 'skpped' typo. An unrecognised value matches nothing and returns an empty page; an empty value is no filter at all. An unknown filter KEY is still HTTP 400.

parameters.name: filter[bad]
parameters.description: 1 = only the runs a human should look at, exactly equivalent to filter[status_code]=failure,warning. This is the contract's is_bad predicate (docs/integration-contract.md 3.4) computed server-side; it is never failure alone, because a run that completed having lost work is the one nobody would otherwise see. 0 is a no-op, not an inversion.

parameters.name: sortBy
parameters.description: Sort field. 'severity' (and '-severity') orders by what the status_code MEANS -- success 0, skipped 1, running 2, unknown 3, warning 4, failure 5 -- so the four spellings of failure land together and an unrecognised or NULL code ranks above running rather than beside success. Severity replaces the default ordering; any other value is appended to it.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: Spatie sort list; accepts the same 'severity' / '-severity' as sortBy, and composes (sort=severity,-id).

status_code.description: The run's own verdict on itself. Legacy rows also hold 'failed' and 'skpped'; an unrecognised value is unknown and must never be read as success.

jobs_count.description: Every job in the run, whatever its state -- the progress denominator. Jobs still running, or with no status_code yet, are counted only here.

jobs_succeeded_count.description: Jobs whose status_code is success (or a legacy synonym).

jobs_warning_count.description: Jobs that finished but degraded: job data was not written, or the decision function could not apply a filter the experiment requested. Nothing else marks them -- they finished -- which is why this count is the one worth showing.

jobs_failed_count.description: Jobs whose status_code is failure (or the legacy 'failed').

jobs_skipped_count.description: Jobs never attempted, normally because an earlier job in the run failed (also the legacy 'skpped').

jobs_degraded_count.description: Jobs whose decision_degraded is true: a filter the crawler REQUESTED did not apply. A count of verdicts, not of statuses -- a NULL verdict is unknown and is counted in neither direction, so 0 is not a clean bill of health unless a verdict exists.

jobs_treatment_lost_count.description: Jobs whose decision_treatment_lost is true: the bot was configured to be treated and produced control-arm data. The alarm. Also counted off a three-state column, so 0 means 'nothing here is KNOWN to have lost its treatment'.
